title: Thanksgiving, Vows, and the Priests' Share
summary: The priestly instructions go on to the guilt offering, which is most holy and eaten by the priests, and settle which priest keeps hides and grain offerings. The peace offering comes in three kinds, thanksgiving, vow, and freewill, each with a time limit for eating the meat, and anyone who eats it while unclean is cut off. Israel must never eat fat or blood, the breast and right thigh of each peace offering go to the priests, and a closing summary names all the offerings the LORD gave at Sinai.
story: This chapter completes the manual of offerings that began in chapter 1. The worshiper's side (1:1-6:7) and the priests' side (6:8-7:38) have now both been covered, and verses 37-38 close the whole unit by naming what has been taught. That summary includes one item Leviticus has not yet described as a procedure, the ordination offering, which Exodus 29 commanded and which Moses will carry out in chapter 8. So the end of the manual points straight into the story that follows. The manual's last word is also its most joyful. The peace offering, with its thanksgiving loaves and its meat shared at the sanctuary, pictures the life Israel was meant to live around God's house once the offerings for sin had done their work.
historical:
The thanksgiving offering of verses 12-15 stands behind many of Israel's prayers. A person rescued from sickness, danger, or enemies would come to the sanctuary, tell the story of God's help, and hold a feast. Psalm 116 ends in exactly that setting: “I will offer to You a sacrifice of thanksgiving and call on the name of the LORD” (Psalm 116:17). Psalm 107:22 calls the rescued to offer such sacrifices, and Jeremiah, facing Jerusalem's ruin, promised a day when the city would again hear “the voices of those bringing thank offerings into the house of the LORD” (Jeremiah 33:11). Vows worked the same way. Someone in trouble promised an offering if God delivered him, then paid it with a feast, as Elkanah did at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:21) and as Jonah promised from inside the fish (Jonah 2:9).

The rules on the priests' share (verses 28-36) reflect a priesthood that owned no farmland and lived from the offerings (Numbers 18:20). Deuteronomy 18:3 assigns the priests a different set of cuts, the shoulder, jowls, and stomach. Some scholars see the two lists as coming from different periods or traditions. Rabbinic tradition harmonized them by applying Deuteronomy's rule to ordinary animals slaughtered for food, and this chapter's rule to sacrifices. The difference is real, and the text does not explain it.
cultural:
The time limits of verses 15-18 had practical effects. A whole ox or sheep was far more meat than a family could eat in a day or two, so the rule pushed the worshiper to invite others: relatives, servants, the Levite, the poor. Deuteronomy pictures such meals as feasts of rejoicing before the LORD with the household and the Levite (Deuteronomy 12:18). Meat left to the third day became piggul, an offensive thing, and the offering no longer counted. The same meat could be dangerous in another way. Proverbs 7:14 has the adulteress lure a young man with the words “I have made my peace offerings; today I have paid my vows,” meaning she had fresh sacrificial meat at home that had to be eaten that day.

The thanksgiving offering also included leavened bread (verse 13). Leaven was never burned on the altar (2:11), but these loaves were not burned; one of each kind went to the priest and the rest was eaten at the feast. The breast was presented as a wave offering, or elevation offering, a gesture of presenting it before the LORD before it passed to the priests. The right thigh was a contribution, a portion set aside from the offering for the priest who handled the blood. Both terms mark food that passed through God's hands on its way to the priests' table.
literary: The chapter completes the series of headings begun in 6:9 with “this is the law of the guilt offering” (verse 1) and “this is the law of the peace offering” (verse 11). Verses 1-10 cover the guilt offering and then settle which priest keeps what. Verses 11-21 set out the three kinds of peace offering and their conditions. Two short speeches addressed to all Israelites follow, one on fat and blood (22-27) and one on the priests' portions (28-36), a reminder that the rules for the sanctuary also governed ordinary kitchens. The chapter closes with a summary of the kind that often ended ancient texts, listing six offerings (burnt, grain, sin, guilt, ordination, and peace) and locating their giving at Mount Sinai. The phrase cut off from his people sounds four times in a short space (verses 20, 21, 25, 27), marking the most serious violations: eating holy food while unclean, and eating fat or blood.

doctrines.note: The thanksgiving offering gave gratitude a public and costly shape. Israel's thanksgiving psalms grew out of this practice, where a rescued person told what God had done in front of family and neighbors and shared a feast. Thanks here is not a private feeling but a testimony.

Holy food must be eaten by clean people, at the proper time, in the proper way. Eating the LORD's portion while unclean is treated as one of the gravest offenses in the chapter, because it drags impurity into direct contact with what belongs to God.
The priests had no land and lived from the altar they served. Paul draws on this pattern when he argues that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from it (1 Corinthians 9:13-14).

words.note: Todah, thanksgiving. It means both the act of acknowledging God's goodness and the sacrifice that expresses it. The word shares a root with the verb for praise and confession. The same word appears in the psalms of thanksgiving, which may have been sung at these very meals.

Karat, to cut, used here in the formula that a person will be cut off from his people. The same verb is used for making a covenant, literally cutting one. Being cut off is the reverse of belonging to the covenant people, though exactly what it involved is debated, as the hard question below explains.

Tenuphah, wave offering, from a verb meaning to move back and forth or to lift. Many scholars think the gesture was a lifting up rather than a side-to-side wave, and some translations call it the elevation offering. Either way, it marked the breast as presented to God before it became the priests' share.

christ: Hebrews takes up the thanksgiving offering in Christian terms: “Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name” (Hebrews 13:15). At the Last Supper Jesus “took the bread, gave thanks and broke it” (Luke 22:19), and the Greek word for giving thanks gave the church one of its names for the meal, the Eucharist. Some scholars have proposed that the thanksgiving meal of Leviticus 7, with its bread, its sacrifice, and its story of rescue told among friends, is one of the Old Testament patterns behind the Lord's Supper; others see the Passover as the main background. Paul's warning about eating the Lord's Supper in an unworthy manner (1 Corinthians 11:27-29) echoes this chapter's concern that holy food be eaten by people who take its holiness seriously. The link is thematic, but it is close: in both, a sacrifice becomes a meal shared by people God has rescued.

hard.q: What does it mean to be cut off from one's people?
hard.a:
The phrase appears four times in this chapter and many times in the Torah, always for serious offenses, and the text never defines it. Interpreters have offered several readings. Some think it meant execution by the community. Others take it as exile or expulsion from the covenant people. Many, including the ancient rabbis, understood it as a penalty carried out by God rather than a human court, whether by early death, by the ending of the offender's family line, or by being separated from his ancestors after death.

The strongest evidence favors God as the one who acts. In Leviticus 20:3 the LORD says of a man who sacrifices a child to Molech, “I will set My face against that man and cut him off from his people,” and he adds that he will do so even if the community fails to punish him (20:4-5). That fits the offenses in this chapter, which usually happened out of sight: eating in private while unclean, or eating forbidden fat at home. No court could police them. The penalty left them in the hands of the God who sees.

questions: The thanksgiving offering turned gratitude into a meal shared with others. When did you last tell someone the story of how God helped you, and what might it look like to celebrate it?
The time limits pushed worshipers to share meat they could not eat alone. What in your life might be meant for sharing rather than storing?
Holy food was forbidden to anyone unclean. How should that shape the way Christians come to the Lord's Table?
